In her late twenties she develops cold- and stress-triggered three-color finger episodes, sees rheumatology (ANA and RF negative, primary Raynaud phenomenon) and a year later cardiology, and is managed conservatively without medication.

documents.title: New Patient Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT – PREVENTIVE

26 y/o woman establishing care. Moving primary care closer to home. Feels well, no complaints today. Last physical about a year ago at her prior office; she recalls a normal Pap there. Records requested, not yet in.

PMH: none. No hospitalizations.
PSH: none.
Meds: none, no supplements.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family hx: mother has Raynaud's. Maternal aunt has lupus. Father healthy as far as she knows. No early heart disease, no cancers she is aware of.
Social: marketing coordinator, mostly desk and client work. Never smoker. Alcohol socially, one or two drinks most weeks. No drug use. Exercises a few times a week (spin classes, walking).

ROS: negative across systems, including no rashes, joint pain, or hand/finger complaints.

Exam: well appearing. Vitals reviewed and normal. HEENT normal, thyroid not enlarged. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly. Skin without rash. Extremities warm, good capillary refill, no edema. Neuro grossly intact. Mood bright. PHQ-2: 0.

Assessment/Plan:
1. Adult wellness exam. Fasting draw this morning: CBC, CMP, lipids. One-time HIV and hepatitis C screens offered and accepted.
2. Cervical screening: will confirm date and result of last Pap from records; due every 3 yrs at her age.
3. Immunizations: confirm Tdap and HPV series from records. Flu shot in the fall.
4. Healthy habits discussed, keep up the exercise.

Return in 1 yr for a physical, sooner prn.

documents.author: PCP

documents.title: Fingers Changing Color
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, since it got cold this winter my fingers keep going numb and turning colors, white first and then kind of blue, then bright red when they warm back up. It's happening a few times a week, outside and sometimes at my desk when a deadline is crunching. My mom has had something like this for years. Is this worth coming in for?

documents.title: RE: Fingers Changing Color
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Yes, I'd like to see you and take a look at your hands. The front desk will reach out for a time next week. In the meantime keep your hands and your core warm. If you ever see a sore or open spot on a fingertip, message me right away.

orders.reason: episodic digital color change, family history of lupus

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: fingers turning white/blue/red in the cold

S: 28F. Since early this winter, attacks of finger numbness with a color sequence: pale/white, then blue, then red as they rewarm. Several times a week. Triggers are cold (walking from the parking lot, holding iced drinks) and stressful moments at work. Each episode passes once she warms up or calms down. Never had a sore, crack or dark spot on a fingertip. Mother has Raynaud's; maternal aunt has lupus. Denies new meds or supplements (takes none). Never smoker.

O: Vitals normal. Hands warm in the exam room, normal color, no digital pitting, ulcers or scars. Skin of fingers soft, not thickened. Radial pulses 2+ bilaterally. Nails normal to inspection. Joints without swelling.

A/P: Episodic triphasic color change with cold and stress, suspect Raynaud phenomenon. Probably primary given her age and mother's history, but with an aunt with lupus I'd like rheumatology to evaluate and decide on testing.
- Referral to rheumatology placed.
- Keep whole body warm, gloves in the cold, rewarm hands in warm water when an attack starts.
- Message for any fingertip sore.

documents.title: Rheumatology Consultation
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT RHEUMATOLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 02/17/2025
Reason for referral: episodic digital color change

Thank you for asking us to see this 28-year-old marketing coordinator.

History: Over the current winter she has had attacks in her fingers several times per week. Cold air and tense periods at work set them off. Her fingers blanch, turn dusky blue, then flush red as circulation returns or the stress resolves, with numbness during the attack. She has had no digital ulcers and no gangrene.

Past medical history: none of note. Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: mother with Raynaud phenomenon; maternal aunt with systemic lupus erythematosus.
Social: never smoker; drinks socially, 1-2 per week; marketing coordinator.

Exam: Vital signs normal. Well appearing. Hands: no skin breakdown or ulceration. Bedside nailfold capillary exam normal, without dilated or dropped-out loops. No sclerodactyly. No telangiectasias. No synovitis.

Labs drawn today: ANA (IFA) negative. Rheumatoid factor negative. (Resulted 02/19/2025.)

Impression: Raynaud phenomenon with features of the primary form: onset in her twenties, no tissue injury, normal nailfolds, negative serologies, and a mother with the same condition. No sign of an associated connective tissue disease today.

Recommendations:
1. Warmth for the whole body, not just the hands: layers, a hat, gloves or mittens outdoors, hand warmers in pockets on cold days.
2. At the onset of an attack, warm the hands under warm water or tuck them under the arms.
3. Strategies to lower stress at work, since that is a clear trigger for her.
4. No medication needed at this time.
5. She should return to us or to you promptly for a fingertip ulcer, new rash, joint swelling or trouble swallowing. Routine follow-up with primary care.

Allergies: NKDA.

Outside Rheumatology

documents.title: Rheumatology Letter
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Madison, I got the rheumatology letter. Your lupus and rheumatoid screening tests were negative and your nailfold exam was normal, which all points to the common primary type of Raynaud's. Their advice matches ours: stay warm all over, gloves and hand warmers, warm water at the start of an attack. No medication for now. We'll check in at your physical.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:

Raynaud's: seen by rheumatology in Feb, primary type, serologies negative. Attacks tapered off once the weather turned; none in the past few weeks. Kept gloves in her bag and a hand warmer at her desk through March and felt it helped. No fingertip sores.

Otherwise well. No meds. NKDA. Never smoker, social drinker.

ROS: no rash, joint swelling, mouth sores or swallowing trouble.

Exam: vitals normal. Well. Heart regular rate, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen benign. Hands: normal color and temperature, no pits or ulcers, nailfolds unremarkable to inspection. No edema. PHQ-2 0.

A/P:
1. Raynaud phenomenon, primary: quiet for the season. Continue warming measures next winter. No drug.
2. Wellness: CBC and CMP today. Pap current (2024). Flu and COVID in the fall.

RTC 1 yr or sooner if attacks become hard to manage.

documents.title: Raynaud's Again
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, my fingers have been bothering me pretty much all year whenever it's cold, and now that it's winter again it's every time I go outside. Same thing as before, they go pale and cold, then bluish, then red and tingly when they warm up, and it goes away by itself after a few minutes. Gloves help but don't stop it. Is there any chance this is a circulation or heart issue? I'd feel better if someone checked.

documents.title: RE: Raynaud's Again
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for the update. Let's get you in this week so I can examine your hands and we can talk about next steps, including a cardiology opinion if you'd like one.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
29F with primary Raynaud phenomenon (rheumatology 2/2025, ANA and RF negative).

S: Over the past year, finger discomfort with cold exposure: fingers go pale and cold, then bluish, then red with tingling on rewarming; settles on its own within minutes. More frequent now that winter is back. Uses gloves and hand warmers with partial relief. No fingertip sores, no rash, no joint pain, no swallowing trouble. Worried this could be a blood vessel or heart problem and would like that looked at.

O: Vitals normal. Hands warm today, no color change, no ulcers or pitting. Radial pulses full and symmetric. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear.

A/P: Raynaud phenomenon, primary, ongoing in winter. Nothing on exam to suggest tissue injury. She'd like a cardiovascular opinion for reassurance, reasonable to obtain.
- Cardiology referral placed.
- Continue warming measures; add a heavier pair of mittens for commuting.
- No medication for now; revisit after cardiology.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOLOGY OUTPATIENT CONSULTATION
Visit date: 02/12/2026
Referred by: primary care physician
Reason: Raynaud phenomenon, patient requests cardiovascular evaluation

Ms. Ouellette is a 29-year-old woman seen in our office for the first time, about a year after a rheumatology evaluation for episodic color change and numbness in the fingers. She comes in midwinter describing a year of intermittent finger discomfort. With cold exposure her fingers first become pale and cool, then turn bluish, and then redden and tingle as they rewarm. Each episode clears without intervention in a matter of minutes.

Prior workup: ANA and rheumatoid factor negative (rheumatology, 02/2025).
Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: mother with Raynaud phenomenon; maternal aunt with SLE.
Social: nonsmoker.

Review of systems: no joint pain, no rash, no difficulty swallowing. Otherwise negative.

Vitals: T 36.9 C (98.4 F), BP 114/72, HR 76, RR 14.
Exam: Normal. Alert, comfortable. Normal jugular venous pressure. Regular rhythm, normal S1 S2, no murmurs, rubs or gallops. Lungs clear. Radial, ulnar, femoral and pedal pulses intact and symmetric. Hands warm with normal color at rest, no ulceration. No edema.

Impression: Raynaud phenomenon, primary, with a normal cardiovascular examination. No findings to suggest structural heart disease or arterial disease.

Plan:
- Continue conservative measures: keep the core and hands warm, gloves and hand warmers, rewarm promptly at the start of an episode, manage work stress where possible.
- No medication recommended.
- No cardiology follow-up needed; return to primary care. Glad to see her again if anything changes.

Thank you for the referral.
Outside Cardiology

documents.title: Cardiology Letter
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Madison, the cardiology note came in. Your heart and circulation exam was normal, and they agree this is the primary type of Raynaud's with no sign of a heart or artery problem. Same plan: warmth and gloves, no medicine needed. We'll go over it at your physical next month.

documents.title: RE: Cardiology Letter
documents.author: patient
documents.body: That's a relief, thank you. See you in March.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL / Raynaud f/u. Turned 30 earlier this month.

Raynaud phenomenon, primary: rheumatology 2/2025 and cardiology 2/2026 both reassuring (serologies negative, normal nailfolds, normal vascular exam). This winter's attacks were frequent in Jan-Feb but brief and manageable with mittens, hand warmers and rewarming under warm water; fewer now that it's milder. No fingertip sores. No rash, joint swelling or swallowing trouble. She is comfortable without medication.

Otherwise well. No meds. NKDA. Never smoker. Social alcohol.

Exam: vitals normal. Well appearing. HEENT normal. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Hands warm, pink, no ulcers, no skin thickening. Distal pulses intact. No edema. PHQ-2 0.

A/P:
1. Raynaud phenomenon, primary: stable. Continue conservative measures. No drug; we can revisit next winter if attacks interfere with work or daily life. Message for any fingertip sore.
2. Wellness: CBC, CMP and lipid panel today. Pap current (due spring 2027). Tdap good until 2029. Flu/COVID next fall.

RTC 1 yr.
